title: The Village That Refused to Give Up

pages.text: By February in the fictional farming village of Nsuom, the dry Harmattan wind had shrunk the nearby seasonal stream into shallow, muddy pools. Worse still, the village’s single old hand-pump had broken down six months earlier because nobody had kept a repair fund. Every morning before school, eleven-year-old Kwame and his classmate Esi saw adults queuing for hours to fetch water from a distant tanker.
sentences: By February in the fictional farming village of Nsuom, the dry Harmattan wind had shrunk the nearby seasonal stream into shallow, muddy pools.
Worse still, the village’s single old hand-pump had broken down six months earlier because nobody had kept a repair fund.
Every morning before school, eleven-year-old Kwame and his classmate Esi saw adults queuing for hours to fetch water from a distant tanker.
pages.alt: In the dry season in Nsuom, eleven-year-old Kwame and Esi watch adults queue with yellow jerrycans beside a broken hand-pump.

pages.text: Under the big baobab tree that evening, Nana Ofori called a community durbar. Neighbours of different faiths—Christian, Muslim and traditional families—sat side by side. One frustrated resident sighed, ‘Perhaps our village is simply unlucky, or we should just wait and pray for early rain.’ Respected elders, the catechist and the imam all shook their heads gently in agreement with Nana Ofori.

pages.alt: At a village durbar under a baobab tree, Nana Ofori and community elders of diverse faiths address the gathered residents.

pages.text: ‘Dry seasons and broken pumps are not a curse or a sign of weak faith,’ Nana Ofori said wisely. ‘Our faith in God teaches us gratitude, honesty, service to our neighbours, and stewardship of the minds and hands God gave us! Prayer gives us hope and unity—and true responsibility means pairing our prayers with sound science, qualified engineers and hard work.’ Everyone clapped in agreement.

pages.alt: Villagers nod and applaud as Nana Ofori calls for combining faith-inspired unity with scientific engineering and shared action.

pages.text: The next day at school, Kwame and Esi’s science teacher demonstrated how a simple classroom filter made of gravel, clean sand and cloth could trap visible leaves and mud from a jar of dirty pond water. ‘Look—the water came out clearer!’ Kwame said. ‘Can people drink it now?’ ‘Never!’ said their teacher firmly. ‘That is a critical life-saving rule of science!’
sentences: The next day at school, Kwame and Esi’s science teacher demonstrated how a simple classroom filter made of gravel, clean sand and cloth could trap visible leaves and mud from a jar of dirty pond water.
‘Look—the water came out clearer!’ Kwame said.
‘Can people drink it now?’ ‘Never!’ said their teacher firmly.
‘That is a critical life-saving rule of science!’
pages.alt: In the Primary 6 classroom, the teacher holds up a sand-and-cloth filter jar and warns students that clear-looking water is STILL not safe to drink.

pages.text: ‘A simple sand and cloth filter only traps large visible particles of dirt,’ the teacher explained. ‘It does NOT remove microscopic pathogens — invisible bacteria, viruses and parasites that cause typhoid, cholera and diarrhoea — and it cannot remove dissolved chemical contaminants! No one should ever drink water from an unverified filter or untreated stream. Safe drinking water requires professional engineering, disinfection and accredited laboratory testing.’

Safe drinking water requires professional engineering, disinfection and accredited laboratory testing.’
pages.alt: A classroom wall chart compares large sand grains with microscopic bacteria and chemical molecules that pass right through a simple filter.

pages.text: That Friday, the Nsuom Water and Sanitation Management Team welcomed Engineer Asante, a licensed hydrogeologist from the Community Water and Sanitation Agency. Kwame and Esi watched from a safe distance as Engineer Asante used geophysical survey instruments to measure electrical resistance deep underground. ‘Beneath dry topsoil,’ Engineer Asante explained, ‘rainwater that soaked into the earth over many years sits in porous fractured rock layers called aquifers!’

pages.alt: Engineer Asante uses geophysical survey cables and instruments on a grassy rise outside the village while Kwame, Esi and Nana Ofori observe.

pages.text: Engineer Asante chose a borehole site on high ground, far uphill from any household latrines, refuse pits or chemical storage so surface runoff could never seep into the well. ‘Good engineering prevents contamination before it starts,’ he told the students. Next, he presented the project budget to the community durbar: drilling the deep borehole, installing a solar-powered submersible pump, overhead storage tanks and four public standpipes would cost 100,000 Ghana cedis.
sentences: Engineer Asante chose a borehole site on high ground, far uphill from any household latrines, refuse pits or chemical storage so surface runoff could never seep into the well.

Next, he presented the project budget to the community durbar: drilling the deep borehole, installing a solar-powered submersible pump, overhead storage tanks and four public standpipes would cost 100,000 Ghana cedis.
pages.alt: Engineer Asante points to a site map showing the borehole on high ground far from latrines, alongside a solar-powered water tank design.

pages.text: The District Assembly and partner water agency approved a matching grant of 64,000 cedis—provided the community raised the remaining 36,000 cedis and proved how they would maintain the pump. Kwame and Esi helped the Water Committee treasurer check the arithmetic on the chalkboard: ‘Nsuom has 200 households. If each household contributes 15 cedis a month, 200 times 15 equals 3,000 cedis a month—and in 12 months, 3,000 times 12 equals 36,000 cedis!’

If each household contributes 15 cedis a month, 200 times 15 equals 3,000 cedis a month—and in 12 months, 3,000 times 12 equals 36,000 cedis!’
pages.alt: At the community noticeboard, Kwame and Esi help the treasurer display the transparent contribution plan for 200 households.

pages.text: Every cedi was recorded in a public ledger book that any resident could inspect, and families who were elderly or facing hardship were supported by neighbours so no one was left out. When the drilling rig arrived, steel casings and a sanitary concrete apron sealed the top of the borehole so dirty surface water could never enter the deep aquifer.
sentences: Every cedi was recorded in a public ledger book that any resident could inspect, and families who were elderly or facing hardship were supported by neighbours so no one was left out.
When the drilling rig arrived, steel casings and a sanitary concrete apron sealed the top of the borehole so dirty surface water could never enter the deep aquifer.
pages.alt: A professional drilling rig completes the sealed concrete apron and solar pump stand on the hill while villagers watch from behind a safety barrier.

pages.text: When clear groundwater pumped up from sixty metres below, nobody drank a drop yet! Engineer Asante collected sterile sample bottles and sent them to an accredited water-quality laboratory to test for bacteria such as E. coli, as well as pH, fluoride, iron and dissolved minerals. Only after the laboratory certificate confirmed the water met Ghana Standards Authority safe drinking-water standards—and the tank’s chlorination unit was set—did Engineer Asante declare the taps safe to open.

pages.alt: Engineer Asante collects water in sterile laboratory sample bottles and later shows Nana Ofori the official laboratory safety certificate.

pages.text: To make sure the new system never broke down like the old hand-pump, the village set aside 500 cedis every month in a dedicated bank maintenance account and trained two local technicians to clean the solar panels and service the valves. On opening day, clean water flowed at four standpipes within walking distance of every compound, and children arrived at school on time every morning!

pages.alt: Clean water flows from the new village standpipe as smiling adults and children fill clean containers and two local technicians inspect the solar panels.

pages.text: In his science notebook, Kwame wrote: What Would You Build, Discover or Change? ‘When we unite across our community, pray with thankful hearts, listen to qualified scientists and engineers, and manage public money honestly,’ Esi said, ‘no problem is too big to solve.’ What shared challenge in your school or neighbourhood could responsible teamwork, science and honest leadership help improve?

activities.question: Why is water that passes through a simple classroom sand-and-cloth filter STILL unsafe to drink?
options: Sand traps mud, but invisible bacteria, viruses and chemicals pass through
Sand turns water into cooking oil
Cloth filters make water too cold to swallow
activities.explanation: A simple sand/cloth filter only removes suspended sediment; safe drinking water requires professional treatment and accredited laboratory testing for pathogens and chemicals.

activities.definition: Underground layers of water-bearing porous rock, sand or gravel from which groundwater can be pumped via a borehole
distractors: Clouds that float high above the ocean
Plastic buckets used to carry rainwater

activities.question: If 200 households contribute 15 cedis per month for 12 months, how much does the community raise toward the 100,000-cedi borehole project?
activities.explanation: 200 × 15 = 3,000 cedis per month; 3,000 × 12 = 36,000 cedis, which combines with the 64,000-cedi grant to equal 100,000 cedis.

activities.question: What did Engineer Asante do BEFORE allowing anyone to drink the clear groundwater from the new borehole?
options: He sent sterile samples to an accredited lab to test for microbes and safety
He tasted the water himself with a wooden spoon
He poured sand into the storage tank
activities.explanation: Even clear groundwater can contain invisible pathogens or excess minerals (like fluoride or iron), so accredited lab testing and disinfection are mandatory.

activities.prompt: Order the steps Nsuom took to build a safe, lasting water supply.
items: Unite the village and consult a CWSA hydrogeologist to survey an aquifer.
Raise transparent funds, drill a sealed borehole and pass lab water tests.
Maintain a monthly repair fund and trained technicians so the pump lasts.

activities.prompt: What Would You Build, Discover or Change? How did Nsuom show that faith, science and honest leadership work together rather than against each other?
